turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, Dr. Smith, I suppose my wife is the one who really pushed for this appointment, but... I am here because I need someone to understand what is actually happening at my job. I work in the mathematical sciences, and right now I am the lead on this massive environmental modeling contract. It is a very complex project, thousands of variables, highly sensitive predictive models, and it requires a lot of precision. 

But recently, I have realized... well, I am pretty sure, actually I am absolutely certain at this point, that the people on that contract have been tracking my specific revisions. Every time I update the system, they are watching my log-ins. And they are going in behind me and deliberately planting errors in the datasets. They alter the parameters just enough to throw off the math, and they are doing it specifically to make it look like I am incompetent, to make it look like I cannot lead the work anymore. It is a coordinated effort to force me out and ruin my reputation. 

I try to explain this to the junior analysts on my team, to show them the anomalies in the code, and they just brush it off. They tell me it is just version-control mistakes, like a merge conflict or a syncing issue with the server. And my wife says the exact same thing, she thinks it is just regular computer glitches and that I am just stressed out about the workload. But I know the math, Dr. Smith. I have been doing this for a long time. The probability of these specific, targeted errors happening by chance right after my updates... it is statistically impossible. They are actively sabotaging my data, and nobody will listen to me about it.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, absolute certainty that colleagues are tracking his log-ins and deliberately planting errors in his datasets to sabotage him, despite his wife and colleagues providing logical alternative explanations (version-control mistakes).

turns.doctor_question: How long have you been noticing these specific patterns of sabotage at your job?
turns.patient_response:
Well, Dr. Smith, if you want the exact timeline... I mean, I can pinpoint it almost to the day because of how our project milestones are structured. The absolute certainty that people on the project are tracking my revisions and planting these errors—that has been there for about the last two months. 

You see, it started right around the time we were doing a major data migration for the hydrological models. I had spent three weekends—three entire weekends, mind you, missing family dinners and working until two in the morning—just calibrating the baseline variables so everything would be perfect for the phase two rollout. And then that Monday, I logged in, and the standard deviation on the runoff coefficients was skewed by a factor of 0.04. Now, to a layman, or even to my wife, 0.04 sounds like absolutely nothing. A rounding error, right? But in a multi-layered predictive model, that cascades. It completely invalidates the entire downstream analysis. 

At first, I thought, okay, maybe it really is a server hiccup, maybe a script didn't compile right. But then it happened the next Tuesday. And then again that Friday. I actually started keeping a physical ledger at my desk, a paper notebook, because I realized I couldn't trust the digital logs on the network anymore. And looking at my ledger, it has been a solid eight weeks—two full months—where I know for a fact they are watching my log-ins. Every single time I commit a change to the repository, within hours, the parameters are altered just enough to make the projections fail. Two months of this, Dr. Smith, and it is just exhausting trying to stay one step ahead of them when they clearly have some sort of backdoor administrative access to my workstations.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses an absolute certainty that colleagues are tracking their revisions, planting errors, and watching their log-ins, which are clear persecutory delusions.

turns.doctor_question: Have you experienced any unusual sensory perceptions, such as hearing voices or sounds that others around you do not seem to hear?
turns.patient_response:
Voices? No, no, Dr. Smith, nothing like that. I mean... I am a mathematician. I deal in hard data, observable facts, numbers on a screen. My hearing is perfectly fine. Actually, my wife, a few years ago, she thought I was losing my hearing because I wouldn't answer her when I was deep into a complex modeling problem at the dining room table, but it was just focus, you know? Pure focus. I was calculating the variance on a localized weather grid and just tuned out the room. 

So, no, I don't hear sounds that aren't there. The only things I hear at work are the cooling fans on the server racks, the hum of the HVAC system, and the junior analysts typing away—which, frankly, they type much too loudly, especially when they are probably the ones actively messing with my code. But voices? Like someone whispering in an empty room or something? Absolutely not. 

If these people who are sabotaging me had anything to say, they certainly wouldn't have the courage to say it out loud anyway. They hide behind their keyboards. They sneak into my directories. They don't speak to me, they just alter the coefficients. So, no, my ears aren't playing tricks on me, Dr. Smith. It is the data that is being manipulated, not my hearing. I mean, if I were hearing voices, well, then maybe I could understand why my wife wanted me to come sit in this chair, but I am just looking at the math. The math is what is... well, screaming at me, metaphorically speaking, because of what they're doing to it. But literally? No. Just the usual office noise. And, of course, the dead silence when I ask my team to explain the statistical anomalies in the log files.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed belief that coworkers are actively sabotaging him, sneaking into his directories, and manipulating his data, indicating persecutory delusions.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly and repeatedly denies hearing voices or sounds that are not there.

turns.doctor_question: Outside of your work environment, have you felt that anyone else—perhaps neighbors, strangers, or even people in the media—is involved in this situation or tracking you in any way?
turns.patient_response:
Well, no, Dr. Smith. I think... I think you might be misunderstanding the exact nature of what I am dealing with here. This isn't some sort of spy movie where I am being followed down the street by men in trench coats, or, you know, having the television broadcast secret messages to me. That would be completely illogical. 

I mean, my neighbors? My wife and I have lived next to the Millers for fifteen years. Gary Miller can barely operate his own automatic sprinkler system, let alone write a script to infiltrate a secure environmental database. He is retired, he plays golf on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and he asks me for help when his WiFi router needs resetting. So no, Gary is certainly not tracking me. And strangers on the street? People in the media? Why on earth would the local news or anyone in the press care about the baseline calibration of a localized hydrological model? They wouldn't. They wouldn't even understand the math if I drew it out on a whiteboard for them, step by step. 

No, this is highly specialized, Dr. Smith. The people who are altering my datasets, they have to have a certain level of clearance. They have to have a specific, working understanding of the project's architecture. You cannot just stumble into a multi-layered predictive model from the street. It requires a secure VPN connection, two-factor authentication, and an assigned administrative user ID within the company's intranet. That is exactly why I know it is the people on the contract. It is an internal, professional sabotage. 

When I leave the office, I am just a regular guy. I go to the grocery store, I walk the dog—we have a golden retriever, actually, my wife insisted we get him last year, absolute menace to her hydrangea bushes, but a good dog—and nobody is looking at me twice. Nobody is following my car on the highway. It is only when I sit down at my workstation and authenticate my session on the network that the surveillance begins. That is the perimeter of this whole situation. It is strictly confined to the project environment because the goal isn't to, I don't know, harass me in my personal life. The goal is to invalidate my mathematical models so they can justify pushing me out of the lead position. If they followed me around my neighborhood, what would that possibly accomplish? Statistically speaking, nothing. It wouldn't change the data. And the data is what they are after. I mean, just last Thursday, I was reviewing the access logs for the remote server, and the timestamp on the intrusion was... well, it just proves my point that this is entirely contained within the company's firewall.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient explicitly describes fixed, detailed beliefs about being surveilled and sabotaged by colleagues at work to invalidate his mathematical models, which indicates persecutory delusions, despite denying that neighbors or the media are involved.

turns.doctor_question: Aside from the time you spend working on these models and documenting the anomalies, how has your ability to manage your daily responsibilities, such as your personal hygiene, household chores, or social commitments, been over these past two months?
turns.patient_response:
Well... it's a matter of resource allocation, isn't it? There are only twenty-four hours in a day, Dr. Smith. When you are spending, say, six to eight of those hours just combing through network logs, line by line, trying to reverse-engineer the corruption they’ve introduced into the baseline coefficients... well, it’s a zero-sum game. Something has to give. 

And, unfortunately, what has given is my actual, scheduled output. I’ve fallen far enough behind on the primary modeling deliverables that—and this is incredibly frustrating, frankly humiliating, to even admit out loud—my firm actually stepped in last week and reassigned pieces of the phase two contract. They just carved it up and handed it over to another group. And my own team? The junior analysts I’m supposed to supervise and mentor? I’ve completely stopped being useful to them. They knock on my door asking for guidance on a simple regression curve or a variance report, and I just... I have to wave them off. I simply don't have the bandwidth to hold their hands when I am fighting a daily war of attrition on my own workstation. 

And as for home... look, when I finally leave the office and get back to the house, I am just cognitively depleted. Completely drained. I mostly just go straight to the den and keep to myself. I don't have the energy for social commitments, I don't want to chat about whatever the Millers are doing next door... I just sit in my chair and try to mentally reconstruct my datasets. 

My wife, bless her, she’s... well, she's bearing the brunt of it, and I know she's worried. She has had to really push me just to keep basic routines going. You mentioned personal hygiene and chores—she literally had to stand in the doorway of the den on Sunday morning and order me to go take a shower because I had been wearing the same shirt since Friday evening. I hadn't even noticed. She’s the one feeding the dog, doing all the dishes, reminding me to shave before I go into the office. It’s just... when your life's work is actively being dismantled right in front of you, remembering to take the recycling bin out to the curb on Tuesday night doesn't exactly register as a high priority, you know what I mean? I just can't focus on the mundane things right now.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient describes failing to finish duties in the workplace, resulting in his firm reassigning his contract deliverables, and failing to complete household chores.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient admits to being forgetful in daily activities, noting his wife has to remind him to shower, shave, and that he forgets to take out the recycling.
symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses fixed, paranoid beliefs that unnamed individuals ('they') are intentionally introducing corruption into his models and actively dismantling his life's work.
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient exhibits social withdrawal, stating he keeps to himself in the den and lacks the energy or desire for social commitments or chatting with neighbors.
symptom_reasoning.S029: The patient reports feeling 'cognitively depleted' and 'completely drained' of energy by the time he gets home.

turns.doctor_question: When you are speaking to your colleagues or your wife about these issues, do they ever tell you that your explanations are difficult to follow or that your thoughts seem to jump around in a way that doesn't make sense?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, not at all. I mean, I am a mathematician, Dr. Smith. Precision is literally my trade. My entire career is built on sequential logic—A leads to B, B leads to C, and if you have a variable, you define it before you introduce it into the equation. So when I speak to people, my thoughts are perfectly ordered. Like a well-structured algorithm. 

When I explain things to my wife—and I try very hard not to burden her with the heavy calculus, obviously, because she doesn't care for the math and it just stresses her out—I lay it out in plain, linear English. I give her the timeline, the cause, and the effect. And with my colleagues? Well, if they ever claim they can't follow me, it is absolutely not because my thoughts are jumping around. It is because they are falling behind on the logic, or, more likely, they are playing dumb because they don't want to admit what's happening on the network. 

I document everything before I even open my mouth. I mean, just last week, when I tried to sit down with the project manager, I didn't just walk in there and start rambling. I brought a binder. A literal three-ring binder, color-coded, tabbed by date and server node. I walked him through the exact sequence of events, starting from the baseline calibration on the fourth of the month, straight through to the anomaly on the twelfth. It was entirely sequential. Chronological. Step one, step two, step three. 

If anything, I am probably too thorough. I over-explain the variables because I know the people I'm dealing with aren't looking at the data as closely as I am. They might get bored, or they might pretend they don't understand because it's easier to ignore a problem than to fix a compromised database, but they never tell me I don't make sense. You don't get to my age and my position by having messy, disorganized thoughts. You just don't. I make sure every single data point is accounted for and verified before I present it. So, if someone says I am hard to follow, it is a deficit in their listening comprehension, or a deliberate choice to ignore the facts, not a problem with my delivery. My explanations are completely solid.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient explicitly denies that his thoughts jump around or that his explanations are difficult to follow, stating his thoughts are perfectly ordered and sequential.
